extracted.intended_audience: scientists, educators, and the informed public interested in science policy and public-health reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: An editorial-style critique of how scientific doctrines should be evaluated for inclusion in education and of the temperament (dogmatism vs. toleration) scientists and institutions should adopt; also addresses public-health reasoning about air/ventilation. Focus is on standards for presenting and teaching scientific ideas and for institutional fidelity to purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as synthesis, not simple averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is not a mere mixture of opposing views — truth is to be sought in a more comprehensive view which combines and reconciles opposing partial views; it is a 'stereoscopic combination' of partial surface views into one objective reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating competing explanations, prefer a reconciliatory, integrative account that combines the correct elements of opposing positions rather than averaging them into a diluted midpoint (anti-pattern: treating conflicting claims as implying a 50/50 compromise such as 'half-and-half').

rubrics_metrics.name: New must include the old; progress by evolution not substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The end and mission of science is not only to discover new truth but to give new and more rational form to old truth — 'the new must include the old — the old must incorporate and assimilate the new.' Progress is by evolution and growth, by derivation, not by successive catastrophes and wholesale substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposed revisions to existing theories for whether they explain and incorporate established observations and insights rather than merely discarding prior knowledge; avoid radical replacement that ignores continuity with well-established facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatism; cultivate tolerant, rational spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Dogmatism, self-opinion, self-conceit are the great bar to establishing a rational philosophy; both old theological and new scientific dogmatisms are opposed to the true rational spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims and authors for openness to critique and humility; value temperate argumentation and willingness to 'try all things' rather than assertions of absolute certainty. Anti-patterns: arrogant certainty, rejection of opposing evidence out of pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test all ideas; hold fast only to what is good and true
rubrics_metrics.description: True wisdom and true philosophy 'tries all things, both old and new, and holds fast only to that which is good and true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require empirical testing and verification before endorsing claims; give equal consideration to both novel and traditional ideas, retaining those supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not teach probable or unverified speculations as fact ('platform science')
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of 'platform science' — that is, propounding unverified and unverifiable speculations as the conclusions of science; what may be merely probable must not be taken as fact or made use of in education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before incorporating a theory into curricula or public policy, assess whether it is 'sufficiently proved.' Avoid presenting hypotheses as settled fact; in education emphasize the distinction between well-established theory and provisional or speculative accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for inclusion in general education: sufficiency of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Virchow's proposed test: only doctrines that are 'perfectly established' (so certain that one could 'pledge our oath to it') should be introduced as part of general education; otherwise they should be withheld until proof is satisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the level of empirical support and consensus as the principal criterion for including a doctrine in elementary or general instruction; recognize practical trade-offs (strict application could exclude many useful, well-supported yet incomplete theories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientists must moderate public advocacy to protect freedom of science
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of science is recent and may be imperiled if scientists do not exercise moderation; lending science to political movements (e.g., socialists/parties) can invite state interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When engaging public advocacy or curricular influence, consider political ramifications and avoid partisan alignment that could provoke backlash and curtail scientific liberty; emphasize careful, non‑dogmatic presentation of scientific findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional fidelity: align institution practice with founding purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should be true to their original purpose (example: the 'Free Academy' meant as a polytechnic/practical high-school) and avoid being subverted into something different by managerial or political capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating institutional decisions, check whether leadership, faculty selection, and curriculum reflect the institution's founding mission; anti-pattern: quiet procedural change that abandons original intent without popular mandate or accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-health reasoning: moving air dilutes, still air concentrates contaminants
rubrics_metrics.description: Stillness of the air (e.g., night-air stagnation) is far more favorable to large aggregation of contagia and local effluvia than rapid air-movement; day-air mobility is analogous to house ventilation, preventing concentration of infectious agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing risks of airborne contamination, consider air movement and ventilation as primary mitigations; favor policies and practices that increase ventilation to prevent localized concentration of effluvia and contagia (anti-pattern: assuming still/night air is inherently purer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider physical/chemical properties of effluvia when evaluating inhalation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Different noxious effluvia diffuse at different rates (e.g., sulphuretted hydrogen diffuses rapidly; carbonic acid more slowly); specific gravity and mobility of air affect hovering over low marshes or cesspools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating environmental-health claims, attend to the chemical and physical behavior of the agents (diffusion rates, volatility, specific gravity) rather than treating all effluvia as behaving similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic humility about microscopic contagia and reliance on best available theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Contagia of infectious diseases are subtile and often undetectable by microscopes; nevertheless, the contagium vivum (germ) theory is the only tenable account of genesis and spread for some infectious diseases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize observational limits but use the most explanatory, empirically grounded theories available; avoid dismissing germ-theory‑type explanations due to current lack of direct visualization—evaluate on explanatory power and indirect evidence.
